sentence: Many decisions arise by gathering noisy evidence until it reaches a threshold or bound.
This process is called bounded evidence accumulation.
In perception, stimulus strength affects decision speed, accuracy, and confidence through this evidence accumulation.
Stimulus strength is measured by the signal-to-noise ratio.
Increasing noise leads to faster decisions, lower accuracy, and paradoxically higher confidence.
Noise here means more variability in the momentary evidence used to decide.
The study used a new sensory manipulation that adds unbiased noise to motion-selective areas in the visual cortex.
This was confirmed by recording neurons in macaque brain areas MT and MST.
In humans and monkeys, increasing noise caused faster decisions and higher confidence with little loss in accuracy.
This effect was seen across different stimulus strengths and was statistically significant when data were pooled.
The size of these effects matched predictions from a bounded evidence accumulation model.
This model explains how motion strength and noise affect choice, speed, and confidence.
The enzyme OspI from Shigella flexneri changes glutamine 100 in UBC13 to glutamate.
This chemical change is called deamidation and is specific to one amino acid in UBC13.
This change silences UBC13’s polyubiquitination activity with TRAF6 and blocks the NF-κB inflammatory response.
Polyubiquitination is a process that helps trigger immune signals through TRAF6 and NF-κB.
Deamidation stops UBC13 from binding to the TRAF6 RING domain without changing UBC13’s shape or enzyme function.
Binding to TRAF6 is needed for UBC13 to activate immune signaling.
Deamidation creates a new internal salt-bridge in UBC13 that competes with a key salt-bridge at the UBC13/TRAF6 interface.
Salt-bridges are bonds between charged parts of proteins that help them stick together.
This salt-bridge competition also disrupts transient interactions needed to form the UBC13/TRAF6 complex.
Transient interactions are temporary contacts that help proteins find and bind each other.
The negative charge on E100 repels the negatively charged surface of TRAF6 RING, further blocking transient interactions.
Electrostatic repulsion occurs when like charges push proteins apart.
This post-translational modification weakens transient complexes and stops protein-protein association.
Post-translational modifications are chemical changes made to proteins after they are made.
Working memory depends on coordinated interactions among large-scale brain networks, especially frontal and parietal regions.
These brain areas communicate across long distances to support memory tasks.
Oscillatory synchronization in the theta frequency range helps coordinate neuronal activity during working memory.
Theta waves are brain rhythms between 4 and 8 Hz that organize activity across brain regions.
Direct causal evidence that oscillatory activity shapes brain network dynamics and behavior in humans is limited.
It is unclear how changing brain waves affects human behavior.
The study used transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to modulate oscillations in a right frontoparietal network supporting working memory.
tACS is a non-invasive electrical method that applies rhythmic currents to specific brain areas.
Synchronous tACS improved working memory performance during high-demand tasks like the 2-back test.
Synchronizing brain waves with tACS made participants respond faster in difficult memory tasks.
The effects of tACS depend on the relative phase of stimulation and the cognitive state, as shown by fMRI.
Brain scans revealed that timing between stimulation and brain activity changes how networks respond.
Synchronous tACS during a verbal working memory task increased parietal brain activity linked to better performance.
Higher activity in the parietal region correlated with faster responses in the memory task.
The relative phase of frontoparietal tACS influences functional connectivity and information flow within the working memory network.
Synchronous stimulation increased frontal-parietal connections, while desynchronous stimulation changed posterior interactions.
Working memory performance is linked to large-scale brain synchronization across a right frontoparietal network activated by the task.
This shows that brain wave timing across distant regions supports demanding memory tasks.
The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is important for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors.
The RSG is a brain area involved in different types of behaviors, including those related to space and other functions.
Researchers used optogenetic circuit mapping in mice to study parallel circuits in the superficial RSG.
This method activates neurons with light to measure how different brain areas connect to the RSG.
The anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum send spatial information that strongly activates low-rheobase (LR) neurons in the RSG.
LR neurons are a special type of pyramidal cell that respond strongly to these spatial inputs.
Nearby regular-spiking (RS) neurons in the RSG are mainly controlled by claustral and anterior cingulate inputs carrying mostly non-spatial information.
RS neurons are a different type of pyramidal cell that respond to non-spatial signals.
Precise layering of axons and dendrites in layer 1 of the RSG allows separate processing of spatial and non-spatial inputs.
This arrangement lets LR and RS neurons receive different input types without overlap.
Thalamocortical synaptic dynamics let LR neurons compute head rotation speed from head direction inputs that do not encode speed.
The way these inputs weaken over time helps LR neurons turn direction signals into speed signals.
These parallel input streams show that LR neurons are well positioned to support spatial orientation computations in the RSG.
LR neurons combine information about direction and speed to help with spatial orientation.
A stable number of petals helps ensure reliable display of reproductive organs and consistent cues for pollinators.
Petals open the flower and attract pollinators, so their number affects how flowers signal to insects.
Arabidopsis thaliana flowers consistently produce four petals across different genetic types.
This shows that petal number is a robust trait in this species.
In contrast, the related species Cardamine hirsuta shows variation in petal number from zero to four.
This means petal number is not stable in Cardamine hirsuta like it is in Arabidopsis thaliana.
Differences in the floral regulator gene APETALA1 explain why petal number is stable in Arabidopsis but variable in Cardamine hirsuta.
APETALA1 is a key gene controlling petal number robustness between these species.
Arabidopsis thaliana APETALA1 makes petal number stable by hiding the effects of other genes that control petal number in Cardamine hirsuta.
These other genes are called quantitative trait loci and normally cause petal number to vary.
The Cardamine hirsuta version of APETALA1 cannot replace the Arabidopsis version to stabilize petal number.
Differences in gene regulation regions of APETALA1 contribute to this failure.
Cardamine hirsuta keeps variable petal number even though natural genetic variation can produce four-petalled flowers.
This shows that genetic variation alone does not fix petal number in this species.
Proper function and repair of the digestive system are vital to most animals.
The digestive system is essential for animal survival, so its proper function and ability to repair damage are critical.
Understanding digestive system function and repair requires an atlas of gene expression and cell types.
An atlas is a detailed map showing which genes are active in which cell types.
Laser-capture microdissection and RNA sequencing were used to study gene activity in the gut of the planarian Schmidtea mediterranea.
This flatworm can regenerate all organs, including the gut.
Hundreds of genes active in the planarian intestine were found that previous methods had missed.
This shows the method is more sensitive than earlier approaches.
The digestive physiology and cell types of Schmidtea mediterranea are similar to those in humans and other animals.
Many genes and cell types are conserved across species.
Spatial laser-capture microdissection revealed that gene expression varies across regions of the planarian intestine.
This regionalization is especially clear in intestinal goblet cells along the medio-lateral axis.
Two transcription factors, gli-1 and RREB2, control regeneration and maintenance of goblet cells in Schmidtea mediterranea.
Gli-1 regulates goblet cell regrowth, while RREB2 supports their survival.
The planarian intestinal transcriptome and methods provide resources to study gut function, repair, and regeneration.
These tools will support future research on digestive systems across animals.
Mitochondria need quality control to remove misfolded proteins and keep working properly.
Misfolded proteins can damage mitochondria and affect their essential functions.
Quality control pathways for misfolded mitochondrial proteins are not well understood.
While cells remove misfolded proteins in general, how this happens in mitochondria is unclear.
Researchers used temperature-sensitive mitochondrial outer membrane proteins in yeast as models to study quality control.
These proteins unfold at higher temperatures, mimicking damaged proteins on mitochondria.
The damaged proteins sen2-1HAts and sam35-2HAts are broken down at the mitochondrial outer membrane by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
The cell tags these proteins with ubiquitin to mark them for destruction by the proteasome.
The ubiquitin ligase Ubr1 tags sen2-1HAts, while San1 tags sam35-2HAts for degradation.
These enzymes attach ubiquitin to the damaged proteins to signal their removal.
Chaperone proteins from the SSA family and Hsp40 Sis1 are needed to degrade both damaged mitochondrial proteins.
Chaperones help recognize misfolded proteins and assist in their tagging for destruction.
The Cdc48-Npl4-Ufd1 complex, Doa1, and the mitochondrial adaptor Ubx2 help remove these damaged proteins from the membrane.
These protein machines extract tagged proteins to deliver them to the proteasome.
This study defines a unique mitochondrial quality control pathway using both cytosolic and mitochondrial factors.
This pathway is different from other cellular quality control systems and works at the mitochondrial outer membrane.
MicroRNAs are small RNAs that regulate gene expression after transcription; miR-9 is abundant in the brain.
Posttranscriptional regulation means controlling gene activity after RNA is made from DNA.
miR-9’s role in dendritic and synaptic development is not well understood despite its known function in early neurons.
Dendrites and synapses are parts of neurons that connect and communicate with other cells.
Researchers created a transgenic mouse with a miRNA sponge to block miR-9 in specific brain areas and times.
A miRNA sponge is a genetic tool that binds and inactivates miR-9 molecules.
Blocking miR-9 in mice reduced dendritic growth and changed synaptic transmission in living neurons.
Synaptic transmission is the process of sending signals between neurons.
miR-9 lowers levels of REST, a protein that represses gene activity, to allow normal dendritic growth.
REST is a transcriptional repressor that blocks genes needed for dendrite development.
Elevated REST protein levels were found in neurons where miR-9 was blocked.
This increase in REST is linked to the observed defects in dendritic growth.
Vector-borne disease transmission peaks at intermediate temperatures and drops at high and low temperatures.
Mosquitoes spread diseases best when it is not too cold or too hot because their survival and reproduction decline outside this range.
We built a mechanistic model to study how temperature affects Ross River virus spread in Australia and the Pacific Islands.
The model uses temperature effects on mosquitoes and the virus to predict transmission patterns.
Ross River virus transmission peaks at 26.4°C and stops below 17.0°C or above 31.5°C.
These temperatures mark the thermal limits where the virus can no longer spread.
The optimal temperature is largely determined by adult mosquito lifespan.
The model predicts year-round virus spread in tropical regions and seasonal spread in temperate areas.
This matches the seasonal peak in human cases seen across Australia.
Temperature suitability varies seasonally, forcing transmission to zero part of the year in temperate zones.
Climate warming will likely increase virus transmission in temperate areas but decrease it in tropical areas near the thermal optimum.
Most Australians live in temperate zones where warming makes conditions better for spread.
In tropical areas, warming may push temperatures above the upper thermal limit for much of the year.
Nonlinear models are needed because small temperature changes can increase or decrease virus spread depending on current temperatures.
The effect of warming varies along the thermal response curve of transmission, causing positive, negligible, or negative impacts on spread.
Motor cortical beta oscillations are brain waves seen in motor cortex, but their behavioral correlates remain unclear.
These oscillations have been reported for decades without a clear link to specific behaviors.
Three macaque monkeys were trained to control their motor cortical beta oscillations using a neurofeedback task before reaching with their arm.
Neurofeedback means the monkeys learned to change their brain waves by watching a cursor linked to beta power.
Monkeys adjusted their beta oscillatory power to target levels before performing arm-reaching movements.
They held the beta power steady to move a cursor, then reached to get a reward.
Lower beta power before reaching was linked to faster movement starts, while higher beta power slowed movement onset.
This effect was consistent across all three monkeys and across trials.
Neural population activity patterns moved farther from movement onset states during beta oscillations, whether induced or natural.
This means neurons were in a state less ready to start moving during high beta periods.
Beta oscillations in motor cortex correspond to neural patterns that slow the start of movement.
This provides a neural basis for why movement onset is delayed after beta activity.
Some viruses like Marburg, KSHV, and Dengue use Nrf2 to help infection, but HIV is blocked by Nrf2 activation.
Before this study, the effect of Nrf2 activation on HIV infection was unknown.
Sulforaphane (SFN), found in cruciferous vegetables, activates Nrf2 and changes cell gene expression.
SFN is produced when these vegetables are damaged, triggering Nrf2 inside cells.
SFN blocks HIV infection in primary macrophages but not in primary T cells.
Macrophages and T cells are different types of immune cells targeted by HIV.
Removing Nrf2 increases HIV infection in macrophages and reduces SFN’s antiviral effect.
This shows Nrf2 is needed for SFN to block HIV in these cells.
SFN blocks HIV after the virus enters macrophages but before viral DNA forms 2-LTR circles.
2-LTR circles are a step before the virus inserts its DNA into the cell genome.
SFN does not increase known antiviral proteins SAMHD1 or MX2 during HIV inhibition.
This means SFN blocks HIV by a different method than these proteins.
Activating Nrf2 can strongly block HIV infection, revealing a new antiviral mechanism.
Aedes-borne arboviruses such as dengue and Zika continue to cause epidemics worldwide.
In the Dominican Republic, a large dengue epidemic was followed closely by Zika virus cases, allowing study of their different transmission drivers.
Researchers used retrospective surveillance data to analyze national outbreaks of dengue, Zika, and Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Retrospective data means looking back at already collected health records.
Dengue cases mostly occurred in people under 20 years old, while Zika infections were spread more evenly across ages.
Dengue attack rates were slightly higher in males than females in the Dominican Republic.
Attack rate means the number of cases per 10,000 people.
Zika infections were much more common in females, with 73.8% of cases and higher age-adjusted attack rates than males.
Age-adjusted rates account for differences in age distribution between sexes.
The basic reproduction number (R0) for Zika was higher in females (1.84) than males (1.72), indicating greater transmission potential among women.
R0 measures how many people one infected person can infect on average.
Guillain-Barre syndrome attack rates were slightly higher in males (0.62 per 10,000) than females (0.57 per 10,000) during the Zika outbreak.
Guillain-Barre syndrome is a nerve disease linked to Zika infection.
Existing dengue immunity appears to have little effect on Zika attack rates at the population level.
Community awareness campaigns likely caused increased reporting of Zika infections among women of reproductive age, though biological susceptibility cannot be excluded.
Health campaigns may have made women more likely to seek care and get diagnosed.
Media campaigns and screening are recommended for women of reproductive age during Zika outbreaks.
When nitrogen is scarce, Anabaena filaments form a one-dimensional pattern of nitrogen-fixing heterocysts spaced by about ten photosynthetic vegetative cells.
Heterocysts are specialized cells that fix nitrogen, while vegetative cells perform photosynthesis.
The HetR protein, essential for heterocyst formation, was studied using a chromosomal hetR-gfp fusion to track its gene expression under both nitrogen-rich and nitrogen-poor conditions.
The hetR-gfp fusion produces a fluorescent signal that shows HetR activity in individual cells.
Expression fluctuations of hetR are linked between nearby cells along Anabaena filaments, with this coupling extending over about two to three cells.
This means cells close to each other show similar patterns of HetR activity.
These linked expression patterns mainly result from molecules moving between cells rather than from recent cell division.
Intercellular molecular transfer allows cells to share regulatory signals affecting HetR levels.
Even under nitrogen-rich conditions, HetR expression fluctuates due to developmental controls and forms clusters that grow after nitrogen removal before resolving into single heterocysts.
Clusters are groups of cells with linked HetR activity that precede the formation of individual heterocysts.
Under nitrogen-rich conditions, the HetR inhibitor PatS, cell communication via the septal protein SepJ, and HetR’s positive feedback regulate hetR expression fluctuations along filaments.
PatS and HetN inhibit heterocyst formation at early and later stages, respectively, while septal proteins SepJ and FraC/FraD differ in how they affect cell communication and hetR expression.

Proteins that activate, inhibit, and enable cell communication work with natural gene expression randomness to control coupled fluctuations that create the one-dimensional pattern in Anabaena filaments.
Humans can learn and store multiple visuomotor mappings when feedback for each mapping is given alternately.
Visuomotor mappings are ways the brain links visual input to hand movements.
People use learned context cues to switch between different stored visuomotor mappings.
Context cues are signals from the environment that help select the right movement pattern.
It is unclear how associative learning between cues and visuomotor mappings generalises to new but similar conditions.
Generalisation means applying learned movements to new situations with related cues.
Participants performed a rapid target-pointing task with visual feedback offsets that depended on the target's shape.
The feedback was shifted sideways, forcing different movements for different shapes.
Target shapes formed a continuous set morphed between spiky and circular shapes.
This created a smooth range of shape cues linked to different movements.
After training, participants were tested without feedback on novel target shapes they had not seen before.
This tested how well they could generalise learned movements to new shapes.
The study compared an explicit linear generalisation hypothesis with an implicit Bayesian learning model predicting categorisation-like generalisation.
The Bayesian model assumes people choose the closest learned movement rather than a smooth rule.
Participants needed explicit awareness of the cue's role to learn and applied the mapping of the trained shape most similar to the current one.
The Bayesian learning model predicted that learning slows down as the number of training pairs increases, which the results confirmed.
The Bayesian learning model matches the data and offers a possible mechanism for learning multiple visuomotor mappings simultaneously.
Vertical control and elimination programs targeting specific neglected tropical diseases can reduce infection prevalence and intensity.
Many NTD-endemic countries lack baseline data needed to start or expand control programs.
Baseline data are basic information needed for planning and advocacy.
Because neglected tropical diseases often overlap geographically, integrated mapping can save resources and improve efficiency.
A new integrated mapping protocol called Integrated Threshold Mapping (ITM) was developed for four NTDs: lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, schistosomiasis, and soil-transmitted helminths.
The ITM protocol is resource-efficient and determines if disease levels have reached thresholds for public health interventions.
Thresholds indicate when action is needed in a specific area called an implementation unit.
ITM uses WHO-recommended disease indicators and age groups, sampling mostly at the district level except for schistosomiasis, which uses sub-district sampling.
WHO indicators are standard signs and measures for each disease.
The ITM protocol was tested by comparing it to WHO mapping methods in one district each in Mali and Senegal.
ITM agreed with WHO methods on interventions for trachoma, lymphatic filariasis, and soil-transmitted helminths but gave more targeted recommendations for schistosomiasis.
ITM was practical, feasible, and showed overall cost savings compared to standard WHO methods.
ITM used fewer vehicles, smaller teams, and took about half the time to implement.
This integrated mapping tool could help start and run needed NTD control programs in endemic countries.
Stem cells naturally reside in specialized environments called niches that support their function.
As organs age, fewer stem cells remain in their supportive niches, but how this happens is not well known.
In fruit flies, Notch signaling increases with age in female germline stem cells, causing them to leave the niche.
Notch signaling is a cell communication pathway that affects cell behavior.
Stem cells with low Notch activity stick better to the niche by having more E-cadherin, a molecule that helps cells attach.
E-cadherin is a protein that strengthens cell-to-cell adhesion.
Increasing Notch signaling in stem cells speeds up their age-related loss from the niche, partly through a protein called Sex lethal.
Sex lethal helps regulate Notch signaling levels in these stem cells.
Blocking Notch signaling in stem cells does not stop their loss with age and does not change BMP signaling, which supports stem cell renewal.
BMP signaling is another pathway that helps stem cells maintain themselves.
Notch activity decreases with age in niche cells that keep stem cells in place, showing Notch controls stem cell retention both inside and outside the stem cells.
Niche cells form the environment that holds stem cells in position.
Notch signaling controls how stem cells stick to their niche as they age, a role also seen in cancer cells where Notch reduces cell adhesion.
HIV infection cannot be cured but can be controlled by using multiple anti-retroviral drugs together.
Each HIV patient has a different viral genotype, so the best drug combination varies per person.
Viral genotype means the genetic makeup of the virus in a patient.
Computer models can predict the best HIV treatment by using viral genetic and clinical data.
Clinical data shows how the virus behaves in the patient.
Current prediction models use only viral genetic sequences and ignore chemical similarities between drugs.
Proteochemometric models combine drug chemical features and viral protein properties to improve resistance predictions.
This approach links how drugs and virus proteins interact to predict drug effectiveness.
The study used a large clinical database with about 300,000 drug-mutant bioactivity data points covering multiple drugs and thousands of HIV mutants.
Bioactivity data measures how well drugs work against different virus variants.
Proteochemometric models predicted drug resistance more accurately than sequence-only models, with errors below 0.5 Log Fold Change.
Log Fold Change measures how much the virus resists a drug compared to normal.
The models confirmed known and found new mutations in HIV Reverse Transcriptase and Protease that cause drug resistance.
When tested on the Stanford HIV resistance database, the models correctly predicted resistance in 84% of cases, better than previous methods at 80%.
These models can accurately predict drug resistance even for new HIV mutants and mixed virus populations.
The models include a reliability measure based on similarity to known virus sequences to inform users about prediction trustworthiness.
Staphylococcus aureus has cell wall-anchored proteins that help it stick to and invade tissues and avoid the immune system.
These proteins contribute to how harmful the bacteria are during skin infections by mediating adhesion, invasion, biofilm formation, and immune evasion.
Clumping factor B (ClfB) is a surface protein that helps S. aureus attach inside the nose by binding to a skin protein called loricrin.
Loricrin is part of the outer skin layer inside the nose called the cornified envelope.
Before this study, the role of ClfB in skin and soft tissue infections (SSTI) was unknown.
ClfB is important for forming abscesses and controlling bacterial numbers early in skin infection by binding to loricrin in the infected tissue.
This binding affects how the abscess forms and how many bacteria grow at the start of infection, as loricrin is expressed within the abscess tissue.
A vaccine targeting ClfB triggers antibody and immune cell responses that protect against S. aureus skin infection.
The vaccine reduced abscess size and bacterial levels in infected mice by inducing both humoral and cellular immune responses.
ClfB is a promising antigen for future vaccines against S. aureus skin and soft tissue infections.
Dengue virus (DENV) causes about 100 million symptomatic infections worldwide each year.
DENV is a common mosquito-borne virus affecting many people globally.
DENV infection can range from mild dengue fever (DF) to severe dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF).
DHF is a more dangerous form of dengue that can threaten life.
Severe dengue symptoms usually appear 5 to 7 days after fever starts during the critical phase.
The reasons why some patients worsen from DF to DHF at this time are not well understood.
Researchers used mass spectrometry to analyze blood serum from adult DF and DHF patients at critical and recovery phases.
This method measures many small molecules called metabolites in the blood.
At the critical phase, 29 metabolites differed between DF and DHF patients, including bile acids, purines, acylcarnitines, phospholipids, and amino acids.
Bile acids were up to five times higher in DHF patients and linked to increased liver injury markers AST and ALT.
AST and ALT are enzymes that indicate liver damage when elevated.
Uric acid, a key antioxidant in blood, was 1.5 times lower in DHF patients than in DF patients.
Lower uric acid may reduce the body's defense against harmful oxidative stress.
During recovery, eight metabolites including the bile acid chenodeoxyglycocholic acid remained altered in DHF patients.
This suggests that liver effects from severe dengue may last beyond the critical phase.
The study found altered metabolic pathways linked to DHF during both critical and recovery phases.
These metabolic changes improve understanding of DHF and point to possible new treatment targets.
The levels of substrate receptor proteins in Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases (CRLs) are tightly controlled to keep all CRL types functional and avoid trapping core components.
Substrate receptors help CRLs recognize targets, so their balance is essential.
Misregulation of substrate receptor parts of CRLs, especially SCF ligases, is linked to diseases including cancer.
F-box proteins, the substrate receptors of SCF ligases, are normally controlled by tagging themselves for destruction within intact SCF complexes.
This tagging leads to their breakdown by the cell's protein recycling system called the proteasome.
When Met30 is not bound to Skp1, due to mutations or cadmium stress, it is rapidly degraded by the cell.
Met30 is a yeast F-box protein that normally binds Skp1 as part of SCF ligases.
A new degradation pathway targets Met30 that is free from Skp1 and requires the cullin protein Cdc53/Cul1 but not Skp1.
This shows that Cdc53 can act independently of Skp1 in degrading Met30.
The SCF core proteins Cdc53, Rbx1, and the enzyme Cdc34 work together to tag unbound Met30 for degradation without Skp1.
This tagging process is called ubiquitylation and marks Met30 for destruction.
Cdc53 and Rbx1 can directly bind Met30 without Skp1, attaching at a region near the F-box domain.
This binding depends on a specific sequence called the degron region that controls Met30 stability.
This Skp1-independent degradation pathway is important for chromosome stability and helps yeast survive heavy metal stress like cadmium.
Cadmium stress causes Met30 to detach from Skp1, increasing the need for this alternative degradation route.
